parts.partTitle: Stop Using extends for Code Reuse

beats.headline: Why is extends the most dangerous keyword in Java?
beats.subline: Implementation inheritance is the tightest coupling in Java and breaks API invariants.
beats.narration: Early object-oriented textbooks told you to extend classes whenever you needed code reuse. In real production systems, implementation inheritance is the tightest coupling in Java and breaks your code in unexpected ways.

beats.title: Modeling Relationships in Java
beats.subtitle: Choose the right coupling level for your architecture

nodes.label: Is-A (extends)
nodes.detail: Subtyping with inherited implementation, fixed at compile time

nodes.label: Has-A (composition)
nodes.detail: Holding reference to another object, swappable at runtime

nodes.label: Can-Do (implements)
nodes.detail: Fulfilling behavioral interface contract without shared state

beats.narration: Always ask what relationship you are modeling. Is-A extends implementation rigidly at compile time. Has-A composes references that swap at runtime. Can-Do implements interface contracts cleanly without shared internal state.

beats.title: SportsCar: Inheritance vs. Composition

top.label: Tightly Coupled Inheritance
points: Exposes engine internals on Car API
Impossible to switch to electric at runtime

bottom.label: Flexible Composition
points: Inject V8, Electric, or Mock engines dynamically
Clean public API with zero leaked methods

beats.narration: Extending CombustionEngine locks your SportsCar to petrol forever and leaks maintenance methods. Composing an Engine interface lets you swap in V8, Electric, or test double engines dynamically while keeping your API clean.

beats.title: API Leakage in Standard Java Properties

steps.explanation: Properties extends Hashtable, inheriting put(Object, Object) and breaking its own String-only contract.
Callers bypass Properties validation by invoking raw inherited Hashtable methods.
getProperty returns null because an Integer was stored, creating silent production failures.

beats.narration: Here is a real JDK mistake: Properties extends Hashtable. Because Hashtable accepts Object keys and values, callers can put an Integer timeout. Later, getProperty silently returns null because it expects a String.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Composition keeps public APIs clean and swappable
Properties extending Hashtable is a classic JDK leak

beats.narration: That is why inheritance leaks. In Part 2, we inspect Joshua Bloch's classic double-counting bug in HashSet to see how superclass self-use breaks subclasses.

parts.partTitle: The Silent Double-Counting Bug in HashSet

beats.headline: How can addAll turn 3 items into 6?
beats.subline: Internal superclass self-use creates silent dynamic dispatch bugs.
beats.narration: Extending a concrete class looks completely innocent until internal self-use destroys your state. This classic Effective Java bug doubles every item added to a custom set without throwing a single error.

beats.title: InstrumentedHashSet Double-Counting Bug

steps.explanation: Increments addCount by 1 and calls super.add(e).
Increments addCount by collection size, then delegates to super.addAll(c).

beats.narration: Look at this InstrumentedHashSet class. It overrides add to increment a counter, and overrides addAll to add the collection size. When you pass a list of three items to addAll, you expect addCount to be three.

beats.title: Dynamic Dispatch Double-Counting Flow
beats.subtitle: How superclass self-use triggers duplicate counting

nodes.label: Dynamic Dispatch Hook
nodes.detail: JVM dispatches this.add back into InstrumentedHashSet

beats.narration: Instead, it prints six! Why? Because AbstractCollection implements addAll by looping and calling this dot add. Dynamic dispatch routes those self-calls right back into your overridden add method, counting every element twice.

beats.title: Execution & JDK Dependency Trap
beats.caption: Why removing addAll overrides still breaks in future JDKs

lines.text: # Run test adding 3 elements via addAll
# Removing addAll override binds you to hidden HashSet internals!
If future JDK updates skip this.add(), your counter silently drops bulk additions!

beats.narration: If you fix this by deleting the addAll override, you tie your correctness to an undocumented implementation detail. If a future JDK update optimizes HashSet to insert entries directly without calling add, your counter breaks silently.

beats.title: The Fragile Base Trap
takeaways: Concrete extension relies on hidden self-use details
Dynamic dispatch routes superclass calls back to subclasses
Fragile base classes break under JDK upgrades
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The Forwarding Class Decorator pattern solution →
beats.narration: That is the Fragile Base Class problem in action. In Part 3, we build the clean Forwarding Class pattern that fixes this bug permanently.

beats.headline: How do you wrap any class without fragile inheritance?
beats.subline: Combine interfaces and forwarding delegates to build bulletproof decorators.
beats.narration: Instead of subclassing concrete collections, implement the Set interface and forward calls to a private delegate. This Decorator pattern decouples your metrics, logging, and validation completely from superclass internals.

beats.title: Reusable ForwardingSet Base

steps.explanation: Implements the behavioral interface while holding a private delegate reference.
Forwards all method calls directly to delegate without modifying behavior.

beats.narration: First, write a reusable ForwardingSet class that implements Set and forwards every method call to an internal delegate. You only write this tedious forwarding boilerplate once for your entire codebase.

beats.title: Bulletproof InstrumentedSet Wrapper

steps.explanation: Only overrides methods needing custom logic; delegates handle the rest.
delegate.addAll executes inside wrapped HashSet, so internal calls stay inside HashSet.

beats.narration: Now extend ForwardingSet in InstrumentedSet. When addAll runs super dot addAll, delegate dot addAll executes inside the wrapped set. Any internal self-use stays inside the delegate, keeping your addCount exact.

beats.title: Inheritance vs. Wrapper Flexibility

top.label: Rigid Inheritance
top.code:
Set<String> set = new InstrumentedHashSet<>();
// Only works with HashSet!
points: Bound to a single concrete class
Susceptible to fragile base class bugs

bottom.label: Universal Forwarding Decorator
points: Wraps HashSet, TreeSet, or LinkedHashSet seamlessly

beats.narration: Even better, your decorator isn't tied to HashSet anymore. You can wrap a HashSet, a TreeSet, or a LinkedHashSet with zero code changes, stacking logging, metrics, or immutability guards at runtime.

beats.title: Forwarding Mastered
takeaways: Wrappers remain unaffected by superclass internal self-use
Decorators wrap any set implementation at runtime

parts.partTitle: Memory Trade-Offs, The SELF Problem & Safe Rules

beats.headline: Does object composition make your Java code slower?
beats.subline: Evaluating low-level memory indirection, callback traps, and safe inheritance guidelines.
beats.narration: Wrapper objects create extra pointer references and small heap headers. Let me inspect the JVM memory layout, explore the hidden SELF problem trap, and outline when inheritance is actually valid.

beats.title: JVM Heap Memory Layout Comparison
beats.subtitle: Single allocation vs pointer indirection

nodes.label: Inheritance Allocation
nodes.detail: Object header plus parent and subclass fields in one contiguous block

nodes.label: Composition Outer Object
nodes.detail: Wrapper object residing in heap holding reference to delegate

nodes.label: Composition Inner Object
nodes.detail: Delegate object holding actual state with secondary header

beats.narration: Inheritance places parent and child fields in one contiguous heap allocation. Composition uses two heap objects, adding object header overhead and pointer indirection. However, HotSpot JIT easily inlines forwarding calls in standard business code.

beats.title: The Callback SELF Problem Trap

top.label: Callback Bypass Issue
points: Inner object registers itself via this

bottom.label: Safe Inheritance Rule
points: Mark concrete classes final unless designed for extension
Subclass skeletal abstract classes (like AbstractList) safely

beats.narration: Beware of the SELF problem: if a wrapped object registers this with callbacks, external notifications bypass your wrapper entirely. Reserve extends for skeletal abstract classes designed for extension, and mark concrete classes final by default.

beats.title: JIT Optimization & Best Practices
beats.caption: HotSpot inlines forwarding wrappers automatically

lines.text: # HotSpot JIT automatically inlines forwarding calls
Indirection overhead is negligible in standard Java applications

beats.narration: Profiling shows HotSpot JIT routinely inlines simple forwarding methods on hot paths. Unless you are writing ultra-low-latency high-frequency trading loops, favoring composition gives you massive modularity with zero observable performance loss.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: HotSpot JIT inlines simple wrapper forwarding methods
Watch out for callbacks bypassing wrappers via the self problem
Mark classes final unless designed and documented for extension
